transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well, doctor... I suppose the main thing, the thing that really made me realize I couldn't just keep going like this, is that I am just so completely, utterly worn out. And I don't mean normal tired, you know? Not the kind of tired you get after a long week or doing yard work. It’s... well, take my house, for instance. It's not big. The bedroom is just down a short little hallway from the kitchen. But lately, I swear to you, just making that walk, just putting one foot in front of the other to go get a glass of tap water... it feels like I’ve been out hauling lumber all day. 

Just lifting these massive, heavy planks, hour after hour in the sun. That's what my bones feel like. My arms, my legs, everything is just made of lead. I'll get to the kitchen counter and just have to lean my weight on it, completely spent, like I just ran a marathon just crossing the carpet. 

And the worst part—the part that really doesn't make any sense to me at all—is that resting doesn't do a damn thing. You’d think if I just went back to bed, laid down for a few hours, closed my eyes, I’d recharge. That's how bodies are supposed to work, right? But I can lie there all day and all night, staring at the ceiling, and resting doesn’t give me anything back. Not a single drop of energy. I wake up feeling just as crushed and drained as when I laid down. It’s just this constant, heavy exhaustion that never, ever lifts, no matter how much I sleep or just sit around in the armchair... I just don't have the strength for anything anymore, and I don't know where it all went.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you used to find pleasurable?

Yeah... yeah, it’s funny you ask that, because it ties right into what I was saying about the exhaustion, really. It’s like... it’s like someone just reached into my chest and flipped a switch, and just completely drained all the color and the life out of everything I used to love. 

I used to be a guy who always had something going on, you know? I had things I genuinely looked forward to every week. Like choir. I’ve been singing in this local choir for years, and Thursday night practice was sacred to me. I loved the harmony, the people, just the feeling of being part of that sound. And when I wasn't doing that, I’d be out in the garage working on cars. Just tinkering, mostly, getting grease under my fingernails, figuring out what was making a rattle... there was such a deep satisfaction in fixing things. Or I'd be down at the rec center playing pickup ball with some guys I’ve known for decades. We aren't as fast as we used to be, but it was just good, honest fun. 

And Sundays... Sundays were my favorite, because that was my day for grilling for the family. I’d fire up the charcoal—always charcoal, never gas—and I’d spend all afternoon out there making ribs, burgers, having the kids and everyone over. I loved feeding people. I really did. 

But now? Doc, I look out the window at that grill sitting on the patio, and it just looks like a useless hunk of metal. I feel absolutely nothing. I can’t make myself care enough to go out there. I can't make myself care about the cars, or the choir, or the basketball games. The guys will text me, you know? My phone will sit there on the coffee table and just buzz and buzz. I’ll look over, I’ll see their names popping up on the screen asking where I am, if I'm coming to practice, if I'm coming to play ball... and I can't even muster up the energy or the interest to type back a single word. I don't answer people's texts. I don't show up. I just sit there and watch the screen go dark, because the thought of trying to pretend I care about any of it just feels completely impossible now.
Have you found yourself feeling like you’re a failure or that you’ve let people down, or do you feel guilty about things more than usual?

Guilty? Oh, God... yes. That’s... I mean, that's practically all I feel anymore when I'm not just feeling totally numb. It’s like this heavy, suffocating blanket that just sits right on my chest, twenty-four hours a day. I look at my wife, and she’s trying so hard to keep everything together, paying the bills, doing the things I should be doing, and I just... I keep thinking about how I’ve completely failed her. And my kids, too. They’re older now, sure, but a family still needs a father, a leader, someone they can look up to and rely on. Instead, they get this... this ghost in an armchair. I failed them. I failed my church, too. I mentioned the choir, but it’s more than just missing practice. It’s the whole congregation, the community... the promises I made to God and to them about being a faithful servant, a reliable man. I just abandoned it all. I let every single one of them down.

But, doctor, it’s... it’s worse than just feeling bad about it. It’s hard to explain, but... it really feels like it’s gone beyond just me making mistakes. You hear about things going wrong around the neighborhood, or sickness going around, or just... just any bad thing happening around us right now. I can’t help but see it for what it is. It’s a punishment. It feels like every single bad thing happening around us is somehow a direct punishment because I wasn't the man I was supposed to be. I was supposed to be the rock for my family. I was supposed to be strong and righteous. And because I failed, because I'm so worthless now, everyone around me is paying the price. I just sit there tracing back every little thing I did wrong over the last thirty years, every time I fell short, and I know it’s my fault. The punishment is here, and it's because of me. I just... I can't stop thinking about it. It just loops and loops in my head, all day long, and I don't know how to make it stop...
Would you say that you feel down, depressed, or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day?

Yeah... yeah, every single day. It's... it’s honestly from the very second my eyes open in the morning. You know how most people wake up and there's that brief moment, just a split second, where your brain is still kind of blank and peaceful before you remember all the things you have to do that day? I don't get that anymore. I wake up, and before I can even process that it's morning, I just have this... this incredibly heavy, hopeless feeling sitting right here in the center of my chest. It’s like a physical weight, like someone parked a truck right on my sternum while I was sleeping. 

It just sets the tone for the entire day, this suffocating darkness that follows me from room to room. I try to get away from it, I really do. Sometimes the house just feels too quiet, too oppressive, so I'll wander out the side door. I told you earlier about how I used to love being out in the garage, tinkering with the cars, getting my hands dirty. Well, now I'll go out there, but I don't touch a single tool. I don't even turn the lights on half the time. I just pull out this old metal folding chair—the one with the torn vinyl seat that I’ve been meaning to throw away for a decade—and I just sit there in the dim light, smelling the old motor oil and the dust. 

And then... I just cry. I'm a fifty-four-year-old man, doctor, and I will just sit out there in the cold garage, burying my face in my hands, sobbing like a child. And the craziest, most frustrating part of it all is that I don't even know what started it. There's no specific thought that triggers it, no bad news I just remembered, nothing like that. It’s just this overwhelming, bottomless despair that pours out of me, and I can't stop it. I'll sit there for God knows how long, just letting the tears fall onto the concrete, feeling completely and utterly broken, and it never really goes away. It just stays with me, dragging me down, all day long...
Have you noticed that your movements have slowed down, or that you can't seem to sit still, like you're physically slowed or restless without meaning to be?

Slowed down... yeah. Yeah, absolutely slowed down. Restless isn't the word for it at all, it's the exact opposite, really. It’s like... well, the best way I can describe it is that it feels like everything I do has slowed down, like my entire body is moving through mud. Just thick, heavy, waist-deep mud, every single minute of the day. 

And it’s not just when I’m trying to walk or do something physical, though that’s bad enough. I mean, just the act of standing up out of that armchair I mentioned earlier... I’ll sit there, and I’ll tell myself, 'Okay, time to get up, time to go to the kitchen,' and my brain sends the signal, but my limbs just... they don't respond right away. It’s like they weigh a thousand pounds each. I have to physically brace myself and push with everything I have just to get upright, and even then, every step is a chore. It takes me ten minutes just to walk down the hallway. 

But it’s not even just the walking, Doc. It’s... it’s my speech, too. It’s how I interact with people. Like my wife, for instance. She’ll come into the room and ask me a completely normal, simple question. Something like, 'Did you want a glass of water?' or 'Did you check the mail?' And I hear her. I hear the question clear as day ringing in my ears. I know exactly what she’s asking me. But then... there's just this massive gap. It takes me such a long, long time to actually get the words out in response. 

I’ll just be sitting there, staring at her, and I can feel my brain trying to form the word 'yes' or 'no', but it’s like the gears are all rusted solid. I can see her standing there, waiting, and I can see that look of worry on her face, and I want to just answer her like a normal person, but I can't force it. The words just won't come out until a long time later, and by then, it’s just... it's pathetic. I used to be quick, you know? I used to banter with the guys on the court, quick on my feet, quick with a comeback. I was sharp. Now I just feel like I'm trapped underwater, watching the world move at normal speed while I'm just... stuck. I'm just dragging myself through this invisible mud from the second I wake up until I finally go back to sleep.
